name: Roman chair / hyperextension bench

lead: A Roman chair supports your hips while you bend forward and raise your torso again. It trains the lower-back erectors, glutes and hamstrings, which people use to hold a more upright stance and build a fuller back and posterior chain.

The chain is loaded back extensions, then stronger spinal erectors and glutes, then better posture and muscle. It is common strength equipment; no trials were found that test it for posture or appearance.

paras: Users do bodyweight extensions, add a held plate for more load, or use the rear pad for sit-ups. It usually sits alongside deadlifts, rows and core work, and strength gains build over weeks of regular training.
Specific safety guidance is not given in the sources consulted and no injury-rate studies were found. People with back injuries usually check with a clinician or coach about loaded back extension.

angle.text: Roman chairs load the lower back, glutes and hamstrings, building the muscle that holds you upright and fills out the back. It is widely used strength equipment; appearance-specific research is limited.

lead: A Roman chair, also called a hyperextension bench, is exercise equipment that supports the body while the user performs movements aimed mainly at the lower back, and also the buttocks, hamstrings and abdominal muscles [1].

In the main exercise, the hyperextension, the user bends forward at the hips to lower the upper body toward the floor and then returns to a straight-back position; bodyweight supplies meaningful resistance and held weights increase the load [1]. Variants include Roman chair sit-ups for the abdominals [1].

The Wikipedia article on the device is flagged as needing more citations and cites no clinical or research studies on effectiveness or risks [1]. No clinical studies of the device for posture or appearance were found.

paras: The article describes the apparatus as a support for the body during exercises, with pads on which the hips or torso rest while the user moves [1].

In hyperextensions the lower back is the primary target [1]. In Roman chair sit-ups the user lies with the hips supported on the rear pad and bends backward, lifting the upper body with the abdominals; the hip flexors stabilise the pelvis and may become prime movers if it moves [1]. The same source also applies the name 'Roman chair' to a wall sit and a squat-like movement that use no apparatus [1].

The bench was added to the wiki because of its association with training the spinal erectors in posture-focused routines. No community threads on it were available for citation, so its place in forum culture is not documented here.
